newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Fed expected to hold interest rates steady.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Fed expected to hold interest rates steady.

text.p: The U.S. Federal Reserve was widely expected to decide to hold interest rates steady at a policy-making meeting on Wednesday amid signs that the see-saw U.S. economy is settling down to an even keel.
With inflation seemingly under control and economic growth slowing to a more sustainable pace, analysts saw little reason for the central bank to alter rates now -- either up or down.
"We don't expect any changes from the Fed," said Barbara Marcin, a vice president at Citibank Global Asset Management. "The economic picture is almost perfectly mixed."
The central bank's Federal Open Market Committee was expected to begin meeting at 9 a.m. (1400 GMT) and to announce its decision sometime around 2:15 p.m. (1915 GMT).
Since trimming short-term rates in January, the Fed has kept policy unchanged as the economy has waxed and waned.
All 37 of Wall Street's premier companies surveyed by Reuters said they expect the central bank to maintain that steady-as-she-goes policy through the end of the year.
It was only seven weeks ago that many of the same firms were betting that the Fed would tighten credit to cool off an economy that seemed to be on the verge of over-heating.
But since then economic growth has slowed markedly, to an annualized rate of 2.2 percent in the third quarter from a rapid 4.7 percent pace in the second.
"While growth will pick up in the fourth quarter, it will remain at a subdued pace," said Chris Varvares, president of St. Louis-based Macroeconomic Advisers.

The slowdown is welcome news for the Fed because it means the economy is settling down to its long-run cruising speed of 2 to 2.5 percent growth per year -- a rate that could be sustained indefinitely without fanning inflation.

It has also proved to be good news for the financial markets. Share prices rose to another record on Wednesday and long-term interest rates dropped to their lowest level since March, partly on expectations the Fed will hold policy steady.
The Wall Street rally was also fuelled by hopes that newly re-elected President Bill Clinton will be able to work out a deal with Congress to balance the debt-ridden federal budget.

Analysts were divided over the outlook for Fed policy in the new year. But an overwhelming majority of those polled by Reuters -- 24 of 37 -- expect the central bank's next move to be an increase in rates to keep inflation in check.
At 5.2 percent, the unemployment rate is hovering around a 7 1/2 year low and is at a level that in the past has presaged stepped-up wage demands from workers, and higher inflation.
"The Fed will have to begin tightening by the spring," said James Glassman, an economist at Chemical Securities on Wall Street.
